claims.text: The identity of X governs protective-oxide behavior through its effect on cation diffusion at the metal–oxide interface.
Al restricts cation mobility more effectively than Si or Mn.
Restricted cation mobility in the Al-containing alloy favors a slow-growing, chemically stable, coherent alumina scale.
The alumina scale resists cracking and spallation.
Si- and Mn-containing variants provide less diffusion control and consequently form less adherent, unstable oxide layers.
The relevant structural mediator is the interfacial microstructure at the metal–oxide boundary.
X-dependent cation diffusion rates dictate oxide-scale continuity and adhesion.
Al has lower relevant cation diffusivity than Si- or Mn-containing variants.
Higher cation diffusion rates in Si- or Mn-containing alloys promote oxide scales prone to cracking and spallation.
Al-containing alloys will exhibit slower oxide-scale growth than Si- and Mn-containing alloys.
Al-containing alloys will exhibit more coherent and adherent protective scales than Si- and Mn-containing alloys.
Si- and Mn-containing alloys are expected to have higher cation mobility and less effective diffusion-barrier properties than Al-containing alloys.
The proposed comparison keeps the Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni proportions fixed while changing X among Si, Mn, and Al.
The hypothesis is scoped to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments.
Phase distribution in multiphase alloys may affect oxidation outcomes.
